planting.note: Mount bare-root on a slab or grow unpotted in a slatted teak basket with little or no medium, hung where the thick silver roots get bright filtered light and maximum air movement; Rothschildiana is a classic large-flowered hybrid of Vanda coerulea and Vanda tricolor and, thanks to its coerulea parentage, grows and flowers best with cooler night temperatures than typical lowland Vanda hybrids.

directions: Grow bare-root in a hanging slatted basket or clay pot with little to no medium so the thick, silver-white aerial roots stay exposed to moving air, providing bright, filtered light and daily wetting followed by rapid drying. Vanda 'Rothschildiana' is one of the classic large-flowered Vanda hybrids, raised by crossing the cooler-growing Himalayan species Vanda coerulea with the warmth-loving Vanda tricolor; it combines the large size and tessellated (checkered) petal pattern inherited from coerulea with richer color and greater vigor from tricolor. The flat, rounded flowers open a rich lavender-blue to amethyst-purple with a darker net-like veining across the petals and sepals, are of heavy waxy substance, and last for weeks on the plant, making the hybrid a long-cultivated favorite for cut-flower use and classic Hawaiian-style leis. Like its parents it is a monopodial epiphyte with strap-shaped leaves and no water-storing pseudobulbs, so the roots need regular misting or dunking in warm weather and must dry within a few hours to avoid rot. Because of its coerulea heritage it tolerates and even benefits from a slightly cooler winter rest (55-60°F nights) compared with typical lowland Vanda hybrids, and it is best grown outdoors year-round only in the warmest, humid, well-ventilated gardens. Non-toxic.

common_name: Spruce Goose Sitka Spruce (Dwarf Mounding Conifer)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; Spruce Goose is an extremely slow-growing dwarf selection of Sitka spruce that, like the species, performs best in cool, humid, coastal-type climates and struggles in hot, dry, continental summers.

directions: Plant container-grown plants in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade. Spruce Goose is a dwarf, irregularly globose to broadly mounding selection of Sitka spruce, believed to have originated as a witches'-broom, prized by conifer collectors for its dense habit of very sharp, stiff, dark green needles carried on a plant that gains only a few inches a year. Its whimsical name echoes the species' own claim to fame — Sitka spruce's exceptional strength-to-weight ratio made it the wood of choice for early aircraft, including Howard Hughes's giant wooden flying boat, nicknamed the 'Spruce Goose.' Like the full-sized species, this dwarf form is native in spirit to the cool, foggy Pacific coastal climate and is happiest with consistent moisture and humidity; it tends to decline in hot, dry, or highly continental summer conditions, and appreciates a site with some protection from harsh afternoon sun in warmer parts of its range. An excellent specimen for rock gardens, conifer collections, and small-space landscapes where a full-sized Sitka spruce would be impossible to accommodate.

common_name: Ravenswing Cow Parsley (Dark Bronze-Black Wild Chervil)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall (or start indoors and transplant in spring) in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Ravenswing is a dark-leaved seed strain that comes largely true from its own seed, but self-sown seedlings can occasionally revert to plain green — rogue out any green-leaved seedlings early to keep a planting reliably dark.

directions: Direct sow in fall, or start indoors and transplant in spring, into moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun. Ravenswing is the most celebrated ornamental selection of cow parsley (wild chervil), grown not for the ferny green foliage of the wild species but for its deep, glossy, chocolate-purple to near-black leaves, which hold their dark color from spring through summer and make it one of the most striking dark-foliage plants for cool-climate borders and woodland edges. In late spring and early summer it sends up tall, branching stems topped with the same frothy, flat-topped clusters of tiny white flowers as the species, which show up beautifully against the dark foliage and are excellent for cutting and as bee and hoverfly forage. It behaves as a short-lived perennial or biennial, self-seeding modestly to maintain a planting over the years; because seedlings segregate for leaf color, remove any that revert to plain green foliage while young to keep the display uniformly dark. Award of Garden Merit winner from the Royal Horticultural Society. As with the species, take care in identification since it closely resembles poisonous relatives such as poison hemlock.

common_name: Heidebraut Purple Moor Grass (Upright Golden Fall Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average to moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; like the species, Heidebraut is slow to establish but improves significantly after its second or third year in the garden.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average to moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Heidebraut ('heather bride' in German) is one of the German plantsman Ernst Pagels's named selections of purple moor grass, prized for its neat, upright, narrow clumping habit and fine-textured foliage — more compact and formal than many Molinia cultivars. In late summer, slender, wiry flower stems rise well above the foliage mound bearing airy, purplish panicles that turn a warm golden-yellow as they mature into fall, creating a luminous, backlit effect when planted where low sun can shine through the seedheads. The foliage itself turns clear gold in autumn before the whole plant collapses cleanly to the ground for winter, making spring clean-up quick and easy. Slow to establish in its first couple of seasons but forms a long-lived, well-behaved, non-invasive clump that is excellent in naturalistic plantings, prairie-style borders, and alongside other Pagels Molinia selections such as 'Transparent' and 'Skyracer'.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Gloire de Marengo Algerian Ivy (Silver-Margined Variegated Ivy)

planting.note: Root cuttings or plant container transplants in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to filtered sun; Gloire de Marengo is less cold-hardy than the plain green species and its variegation can scorch in harsh winter sun and wind, so give it a sheltered site in colder parts of its range.

directions: Plant cuttings in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun; Gloire de Marengo is the classic, most widely grown variegated form of Algerian ivy, valued for large, glossy, dark green leaves broadly marbled with silvery gray-green and edged in creamy white — one of the most handsome variegated foliage vines for shady walls, fences, hanging baskets, and groundcover in mild climates. It shares the large-leaved, heat- and drought-tolerant character of the species once established, but is somewhat less cold hardy and more prone to leaf scorch from strong winter sun or drying wind, so it benefits from a sheltered exposure in the cooler parts of its range. Like other ivies it climbs readily by aerial roots and can be trained on supports or left to trail, but it spreads less aggressively than English ivy. Occasional shoots that revert to solid green should be pruned out to keep the variegation strong. Plant away from natural areas to avoid escape.

common_name: Aureomarginata Ventricosa Hosta (Yellow-Margined Blue Plantain Lily)

planting.note: Plant container stock or divisions in spring in rich, evenly moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; like the species, Aureomarginata is one of the more heat-tolerant variegated hostas, performing reasonably well into zone 9 where many large-leaved hostas struggle.

directions: Plant in rich, consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to full shade. Aureomarginata is one of the oldest and best-known variegated selections of Hosta ventricosa, bearing the species' glossy, deep-green, broadly heart-shaped, quilted leaves edged in an irregular band of creamy yellow to gold that brightens as the season progresses. Like the straight species it tolerates deeper shade and more summer heat than many hostas, and produces the same striking deep-violet to violet-purple flowers on tall scapes in mid- to late summer, held well above the foliage mound. Because it is a chimeral variegation, occasional shoots may revert to solid green or lose the margin; remove reverted growth at the base as soon as it appears to keep the clump uniformly variegated. Otherwise it is as tough and low-maintenance as the species, increasing steadily by division over the years.

common_name: Newport Flowering Plum (Cold-Hardy Purple-Leaf Ornamental Plum)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Newport is valued as one of the most cold-hardy purple-leaf plum selections, reliably grown into zone 4 where cultivars like 'Thundercloud' can suffer winter dieback.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Newport is a compact, cold-hardy purple-leaf plum selection prized for foliage that emerges reddish-purple in spring and holds its color through the season better in cool climates than many purple-leaf plum cultivars, sometimes fading toward bronze-green in extreme summer heat. Single, light pink flowers open in very early spring before the leaves, on a smaller, rounder-headed tree than the species. Small, purplish-red fruit forms in summer and is technically edible, though the tree is grown almost exclusively as an ornamental. Newport's standout trait is cold hardiness — it tolerates winters into zone 4, making it one of the few purple-foliage flowering plums reliable in the Upper Midwest and Northeast, where less hardy purple-leaf cultivars are prone to dieback. Short-lived compared with many landscape trees (15-25 years) but fast-growing and dependably floriferous; prune to remove crossing or damaged branches after flowering.

common_name: Glauca Blue Atlas Cedar (Classic Upright Silver-Blue Cedar)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped grafted trees in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; give Glauca plenty of room, since it eventually becomes a large, wide-spreading specimen tree unsuited to small residential lots.

directions: Plant grafted, container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun, where drainage is excellent; heavy, wet clay causes rapid decline. Glauca is the classic, most widely planted blue-needled Atlas cedar selection, valued for intensely silvery-blue to blue-gray foliage carried on stiff, ascending branches that build, over decades, into a broad, flat-topped, pyramidal to irregularly spreading crown — one of the bluest and most architectural conifers grown in temperate gardens. Unlike the cascading, ground-hugging or trained forms of the weeping cultivar 'Glauca Pendula', Glauca grows as a strongly upright tree from the start and needs no staking to develop a central leader. Large, barrel-shaped, upright cones take about two years to mature and add ornamental interest to older specimens. Highly drought-tolerant once established, reflecting its native origin on the dry, rocky slopes of Morocco and Algeria's Atlas Mountains, and hardier to cold than the related deodar cedar. Best used as a specimen or focal-point tree where its eventual large size and wide crown can be appreciated without crowding.
